service.name: Wedding cocktail hour music
service.serviceType: Live music for wedding cocktail hours
service.description: Jazz duo, acoustic duo and solo guitarist bookings for wedding cocktail hours across Denver, the Front Range and the Colorado mountain corridor.

faqs.q: Is there music during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Yes, at nearly every wedding. The hour between the ceremony and dinner is when guests stand with a first drink and meet each other, and something fills it. Live players, a DJ or a playlist through the venue's own system are the three ways it gets filled, and they do not land the same way.

faqs.q: Do you need music during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: You need something, and live players are the version guests register. Silence in that hour reads as a gap in the day, because the couple is away for photographs and nothing else is happening yet. A duo at conversation volume covers the turn without asking anyone for their attention.

faqs.q: What kind of music should play during cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Jazz standards and singer-songwriter covers, songs guests recognize without having to name. The repertoire matters less than the level. Upright bass and guitar leaves space in the middle of the sound where conversation sits, which is the actual job of the hour.

faqs.q: How many songs for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Roughly fifteen to twenty for a 60-minute hour and closer to thirty for 90 minutes, because a standard runs three to four minutes. Live players do not work to a count: sets run continuously and tunes stretch or shorten to the crowd, so the number is an outcome rather than a plan. Song counts are a playlist problem.

faqs.q: Will anyone actually notice the music?
faqs.a: Not consciously, and that is the hour going right. Guests notice that the evening felt hosted, not which tunes played. What they do register is two people playing thirty feet away: a live act at conversation volume changes how a space feels without ever becoming the thing being watched.

That is exactly what the level is set for. Cocktail and dinner sets run 65 to 72 dBA at the nearest table, a volume two people who have just met can talk across without leaning in. A band playing this hour at dance-floor level has guests shouting introductions over a first drink.

faqs.q: Instrumental or vocals for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Instrumental, for most of the hour. A voice pulls attention to the words, and guests who are mid-introduction feel that as competition. Upright bass and guitar leaves the middle of the sound clear. Where a wedding wants a voice anyway, Tejas Singh fronts the hour and the level comes down to match.

faqs.q: Is a duo overkill for 60 to 70 guests?
faqs.a: No. Two players are the right size for that count, holding 65 to 72 dBA across a crowd from twenty at one table to eighty across ten. What is overkill at that headcount is a four-piece with horns. A duo can shade its volume live, which a bigger build cannot do as far.

faqs.q: How long is a wedding cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Sixty minutes is standard. It stretches to 90 when the venue turns one space from ceremony to reception, because guests cannot go back in until the flip is done. Added time costs what the earlier time did, in 30-minute increments, and there is no overtime rate.

faqs.q: Should we book a band or a DJ for cocktail hour?
faqs.a: Two players, for this hour. A duo reads the crowd, takes a request, and lands at a volume people can talk across. A DJ earns its fee later, carrying the dance floor after dinner. For this one hour they are not close, and after dinner the answer flips.

faqs.q: Can one booking cover the cocktail hour and dinner?
faqs.a: Yes. The same two players carry cocktails and dinner on one line of the contract, with sound included and the whole block quoted as one figure for your date. One load-in and one invoice, and the hour never goes silent between sets.
